{{Short description|Test of normality in frequentist statistics}}
{{Distinguish|text=the [[likelihood-ratio test]], which is sometimes referred to as Wilks test}}
The '''Shapiro–Wilk test''' is a [[Normality test|test of normality]]. It was published in 1965 by [[Samuel Sanford Shapiro]] and [[Martin Wilk]].<ref name="Shapiro–Wilk" />

==Theory==
The Shapiro–Wilk test tests the [[null hypothesis]] that a [[statistical sample|sample]] ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''n''</sub> came from a [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] population. The [[test statistic]] is

<math display="block">W = \frac{{\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^n a_i x_{(i)}\right)}^2}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n {\left(x_i-\overline{x}\right)}^2},</math>

where

* <math>x_{(i)}</math> with parentheses enclosing the subscript index ''i'' is the ''i''th [[order statistic]], i.e., the ''i''th-smallest number in the sample (not to be confused with <math>x_i</math>).
* <math>\overline{x} = \left( x_1 + \cdots + x_n \right) / n</math> is the sample mean.

The coefficients <math>a_i</math> are given by:<ref name="Shapiro–Wilk">{{cite journal
 |last1=Shapiro |first1=S. S.
 |last2=Wilk |first2=M. B. |author-link2=Martin Wilk
 |year=1965
 |title=An analysis of variance test for normality (complete samples)
 |journal=[[Biometrika]]
 |volume=52 |issue=3–4 |pages=591–611
 |doi=10.1093/biomet/52.3-4.591 |jstor=2333709 | mr = 205384
}} p.&nbsp;593</ref>
<math display="block">(a_1,\dots,a_n) = {m^{\mathsf{T}} V^{-1} \over C},</math>
where ''C'' is a [[vector norm]]:<ref name="mit">{{cite web |title=The Shapiro-Wilk and related tests for normality |author=Richard M. Dudley|authorlink=Richard M. Dudley |year=2015 |url=https://math.mit.edu/~rmd/465/shapiro.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240729131413/https://math.mit.edu/~rmd/465/shapiro.pdf |access-date=2024-07-29 |archive-date=29 July 2024 }} </ref>
<math display="block">C = \left\| V^{-1} m \right\| = {\left(m^{\mathsf{T}} V^{-1} V^{-1} m\right)}^{1/2}</math>
and the vector ''m'',
<math display="block">m = (m_1,\dots,m_n)^{\mathsf{T}}</math>
is made of the [[expected value]]s of the [[order statistic]]s of [[independent and identically distributed random variables]] sampled from the standard normal distribution; finally, <math>V</math> is the [[covariance matrix]] of those normal order statistics.<ref name="DavisStephens1978">{{cite tech report |last1=Davis |first1=C. S. |last2=Stephens |first2=M. A. |title=The covariance matrix of normal order statistics |number=Technical Report No. 14 |institution=Department of Statistics, Stanford University, Stanford, California |year=1978 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221004220433/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a053857.pdf |access-date=2022-10-04 }}</ref>

There is no name for the distribution of <math>W</math>. The cutoff values for the statistics are calculated through [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo simulations]].<ref name="mit"/>

==Interpretation==
The [[Statistical hypothesis testing|null-hypothesis]] of this test is that the population is normally distributed. If the [[p-value|''p'' value]] is less than the chosen [[alpha level]], then the null hypothesis is rejected and there is evidence that the data tested are not normally distributed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.jmp.com/support/notes/35/406.html |title=How do I interpret the Shapiro–Wilk test for normality? |work=JMP |year=2004 |access-date=March 24, 2012 |archive-date=May 25, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120525103314/http://www.jmp.com/support/notes/35/406.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Like most [[statistical significance|statistical significance tests]], if the sample size is sufficiently large this test may detect even trivial departures from the null hypothesis (i.e., although there may be some [[Statistical significance#Effect size|statistically significant effect]], it may be too small to be of any practical significance); thus, additional investigation of the ''effect size'' is typically advisable, e.g., a [[Q–Q plot]] in this case.<ref>{{cite book|last=Field|first=Andy|title=Discovering statistics using SPSS |year=2009|publisher=SAGE Publications|location=Los Angeles [i.e. Thousand Oaks, Calif.]|isbn=978-1-84787-906-6|page=143|edition=3rd}}</ref>

==Power analysis==
Monte Carlo simulations have demonstrated in practically relevant settings that Shapiro–Wilk has the best [[Statistical power|power]] for a given [[Statistical significance|significance]], followed closely by [[Anderson–Darling test|Anderson–Darling]] when comparing the Shapiro–Wilk, [[Kolmogorov–Smirnov test|Kolmogorov–Smirnov]], and [[Lilliefors test|Lilliefors]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Razali|first=Nornadiah|author2=Wah, Yap Bee |title=Power comparisons of Shapiro–Wilk, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Lilliefors and Anderson–Darling tests|journal=Journal of Statistical Modeling and Analytics|year=2011|volume=2|issue=1|pages=21–33|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267205556|access-date=30 March 2017}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=October 2024}}

==Approximation==
The main bottleneck in the use of this method for higher sample sizes lies in the calculation of the coefficients vector ''a'', more specifically in the size of ''V'' which requires the storage of {{math|1=''n'' + ''n''(''n'' + 1)/2}} numbers at minimum.<ref name=Royston/> The original 1965 publication included values of ''V'' up to {{nowrap|1=''n'' = 50}} for this purpose<ref name=RG/> (though the values for {{math|1=''n'' &leq; 20}} was incorrect).<ref name=Royston/> Another issue is the requirement for a precalculated set of cutoffs for ''W'' at a given ''n'' and alpha-level.<ref name=Royston/> It is also known that the [[Shapiro–Francia test]] is asymptotically equivalent, but it is not close enough at practical ''n''.<ref name=Royston/>

In 1982 Royston provided a more correct method of calculating ''m'' and a lognormal approximation of ''W'' up to {{math|1=''n'' = 2000}}, which could be used with an existing approximation of ''V'', but the quadratic limitation on ''V'' remained. In 1991, Royston published a polynomial fit for <math>a_n-c_n</math>, where <math display=inline>c_i=\left(\tilde{m}^\intercal \tilde{m}\right)^{-1/2} \tilde{m}_i</math> and <math display=inline>\tilde{m}_i = \Phi^{-1}\left[(i-\frac{3}{8})/(n+{1}{4})\right]</math> (Welsberg&ndash;Bingham statistic, an approximation of Shapiro-Francia) up to {{math|1=''n'' = 1000}}. Combined with lognormal fits for ''W'' given <math>\tilde{a}</math>, it appears to work well at {{math|1=''n'' = 5000}} by comparison with published critical points.<ref name=Royston>{{cite journal|last=Royston|first=Patrick|title=Approximating the Shapiro–Wilk ''W''-test for non-normality|journal=Statistics and Computing|date=September 1992|volume=2|issue=3|pages=117–119|doi=10.1007/BF01891203|s2cid=122446146 }}</ref> The 1991 technique is used in several software packages including [https://www.graphpad.com/guides/prism/latest/statistics/stat_choosing_a_normality_test.htm GraphPad Prism],  Stata,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Royston|first=Patrick|title=Shapiro–Wilk and Shapiro–Francia Tests|journal=Stata Technical Bulletin, StataCorp LP|volume=1|issue=3}}</ref><ref>[https://www.stata.com/manuals15/rswilk.pdf Shapiro–Wilk and Shapiro–Francia tests for normality]</ref> SPSS, and SAS.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Park|first=Hun Myoung|title=Univariate Analysis and Normality Test Using SAS, Stata, and SPSS|journal=[working paper]|date=2002–2008|hdl=2022/19742 |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2022/19742|access-date=29 July 2023}}</ref>

Rahman and Govidarajulu provided an approximation of ''W'' up to {{math|1=''n'' = 5000}}, though they appear unaware of Royston's 1991 work.<ref name=RG>{{cite journal|last1=Rahman|last2=Govidarajulu|title=A modification of the test of Shapiro and Wilk for normality|journal=Journal of Applied Statistics|date=1997|volume=24|issue=2|pages=219–236|doi=10.1080/02664769723828 |bibcode=1997JApSt..24..219R }}</ref>
